stages.title: Bertrand Russell and analytic philosophy
stages.hook: "The present King of France is bald." Is this sentence true, false, or neither? Write down your answer and your reason.
explain: Bertrand Russell (1872 to 1970), a British philosopher, logician and social critic, helped found analytic philosophy, which stresses clarity, logical analysis and close attention to language. With Alfred North Whitehead he wrote Principia Mathematica (1910 to 1913), an attempt to derive mathematics from logic. In 1901 he found Russell's paradox: consider the set of all sets that are not members of themselves. If it is a member of itself, then it is not; if it is not, then it is. This showed that naive set theory leads to contradiction and spurred new foundations.

In "On Denoting" (1905), Russell offered the theory of descriptions. A sentence such as "The present King of France is bald" is analysed as claiming that there is exactly one King of France and he is bald. Since there is no such king, the sentence is false (on Russell's analysis) rather than meaningless. The analysis reveals logical form beneath grammatical form. Critics, notably P. F. Strawson, argued that such a sentence presupposes a king and is better seen as lacking a truth value.

Russell distinguished knowledge by acquaintance (direct awareness) from knowledge by description. In The Problems of Philosophy (1912) he examined appearance and reality, induction and the value of philosophy. He also wrote on social issues, opposed the First World War (and was imprisoned in 1918), and received the 1950 Nobel Prize in Literature. His "teapot" analogy argues that the burden of proof lies on whoever makes an unfalsifiable claim.

example.q: Show how Russell analyses "The King of France is bald".
steps: Claim 1: there is a King of France.
Claim 2: there is at most one.
Claim 3: whoever is King is bald.
Claim 1 is false, so the whole statement is false.
example.a: Russell: false, because the existence claim fails.

analogies.tech: Reading code reveals logical structure beneath the way a program looks on screen, like logical form beneath grammar.
analogies.city: A map symbol for a bridge that was never built shows how a description can be meaningful while nothing matches it.
analogies.music: A score can be written and analysed even if never performed, like a description with no matching object.

stages.mnemonic: Russell: strip the sentence to its logic; paradox cracks the sets.
terms: A tradition stressing clarity, argument and logical analysis of language and concepts.
The contradiction arising from the set of all sets that do not contain themselves.
Russell's analysis of phrases like "the F" as existence, uniqueness and predication.
The underlying logical structure of a sentence, which may differ from its grammar.

misc.wrong: Russell's analysis shows that sentences about non-existent things are meaningless.
misc.right: On Russell's account they are meaningful and false. Strawson and others disagree and think they lack a truth value.

stages.limits: Russell's views changed over his long career (logicism, logical atomism, neutral monism), and his theory of descriptions remains debated.

trip.prompt: Find Russell's paradox and the theory of descriptions.

questions.q: What does Russell's paradox show?
o: Naive set theory leads to contradiction
That sets are not a useful idea in mathematics
That arithmetic itself is inconsistent
That logic cannot be applied to mathematics
questions.why: It required more careful axioms for set theory.

questions.q: What did Principia Mathematica aim at?
o: Deriving mathematics from logic
Describing the physical laws of the universe
Classifying kinds of numbers by size
Proving that arithmetic is a matter of opinion
questions.why: It was a logicist project by Russell and Whitehead.

questions.q: On Russell's analysis, "The present King of France is bald" is...
o: False
True
Meaningless
A question

questions.q: Strawson objected that such sentences...
o: Presuppose a king and may lack a truth value
Are true because the king would be bald
Are mathematical claims about sets
Are commands to a king

questions.q: Knowledge by acquaintance is...
o: Direct awareness
Knowledge from books
Guessing
Rumour

questions.q: Russell's teapot is used to argue that...
o: The burden of proof is on those making unfalsifiable claims
Evidence about celestial teapots would be extremely hard to find in space
Evidence is of no use in philosophy
Unfalsifiable claims need no support

questions.q: Why is "the set of all sets that are not members of themselves" paradoxical?
o: Membership leads to non-membership and vice versa
The set would have to be empty
The set would have to be infinite
The set is not well defined in ordinary mathematical language at all

questions.q: Match each item to its role.
pairs: Critic of the theory of descriptions
Earlier logicist whose system the paradox affected

questions.q: Explain how the theory of descriptions treats a sentence about a non-existent entity.
questions.model: It rewrites "the F is G" as claims that there is exactly one F and it is G; if nothing is F, the existence claim is false, so the sentence is false.
questions.why: Russell treats it as false, not nonsense.

questions.q: A speaker says "The tallest person in the room is bald" and the room is empty. Apply Russell's analysis:
o: False, since no tallest person exists there
True, since there is nobody taller
Meaningless, since the room is empty
A command to find the tallest person

panel.q: Why is the move from grammar to logical form philosophically useful?
o: It can expose hidden assumptions and ambiguities
It removes all disagreement among philosophers
It proves facts about the world by logic alone
It replaces the need for evidence

panel.q: Give one reason someone might prefer Strawson's view over Russell's.
panel.model: In ordinary speech, saying the King of France is bald seems to presuppose there is a king, so we may feel the sentence misfires rather than is simply false.

panel.q: Which statement fits the analytic tradition?
o: Philosophical problems can be clarified by analysing language and logic
Philosophical problems are best treated as poetry rather than argument
Evidence has no place in philosophy
Philosophical problems should be left alone

teach.model: Russell used logic to analyse language and mathematics. His paradox exposed trouble in set theory, and his theory of descriptions treats phrases like "the King of France" as existence claims. Critics such as Strawson disagree. For example, the King of France sentence.

points.ask: What is the theory of descriptions?

stages.title: Ludwig Wittgenstein and philosophy of language
stages.hook: What is a game? Try to give a definition that covers chess, football, patience and a child throwing a ball against a wall, but excludes everything else. Can you?
explain: Ludwig Wittgenstein (1889 to 1951), an Austrian-British philosopher, is known for two major phases. In the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1921) he proposed a picture theory: a proposition pictures a possible state of affairs, sharing its logical form. Meaningful language states facts; what cannot be said (such as ethics and the mystical) can only be shown. The book ends with the line often translated as "Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent."

In Philosophical Investigations (published 1953, after his death) he criticised his early view. Meaning, he argued, is often found in use: words are tools used in language-games within forms of life. The term "game" illustrates family resemblance: instances overlap in many features without one shared essence. He examined rule-following and argued against the idea of a purely private language, a language whose words refer only to the speaker's inner sensations and which no one else could in principle understand. Interpretations of the argument are disputed.

He saw philosophical problems as often arising from misusing language and wrote that philosophy should help "show the fly the way out of the fly-bottle". His influence reaches philosophy of mind, language, logic and the social sciences. Scholars debate how continuous his early and late work is, and whether the Philosophical Investigations should be read as therapy or as offering positive theory.

example.q: How would the later Wittgenstein examine the word "game"?
steps: Look at actual cases.
Notice overlaps, not a single common feature.
Conclude that "game" has family resemblance, not a strict definition.
example.a: Concept with overlapping similarities, not one shared essence.

analogies.city: People in a city speak many dialects but are understood through shared use.
analogies.music: Genres overlap without one defining feature.
analogies.home: Members of a family share eyes, laugh or walk, but no one feature is common to all.

stages.mnemonic: Meaning is use; games share a family look, not one definition.
terms: The early view that propositions picture possible facts.
Wittgenstein's term for a context of language use tied to activity.
Overlapping similarities among instances of a concept, without a common essence.
His argument against a language whose meanings only one speaker could know.

misc.wrong: Wittgenstein simply rejected his earlier work as nonsense.
misc.right: He criticised parts of it, but scholars disagree about the continuity between early and late thought.

stages.limits: Many central ideas in the Investigations, including the private language argument, are interpreted in conflicting ways.

trip.prompt: Find the explanations of "language-game" and "family resemblance".

questions.q: The Tractatus proposes that propositions...
o: Picture possible states of affairs
Express feelings and attitudes only
Are always commands to act
Are never true or false

questions.q: "Meaning is use" is associated with...
o: The later Wittgenstein
The Tractatus, in its picture theory
Aristotle, in his Metaphysics
Descartes, in the Meditations

questions.q: Family resemblance suggests that...
o: Instances may be linked by overlapping features without one essence
All members of a concept must share at least one single common feature
Words need no shared meaning to work
Games cannot be grouped under a word

questions.q: The private language argument targets...
o: A language only one speaker could understand in principle
Any foreign language that a learner has not yet had time to master
Sign languages used by the deaf
Computer languages used in programming

questions.q: A language-game is...
o: A context in which language is used within an activity
A board game played with a rulebook that is made up of words
A grammar book of correct sentences
A translation from one language into another

questions.q: Which sentence best describes how Wittgenstein sees many philosophical problems?
o: They arise from misusing language
They are all easy
They are solved by measurement
They are about weather
questions.why: He saw confusion arising from language.

questions.q: Match work and idea.
A friend says "Every concept must have necessary and sufficient conditions". How might the later Wittgenstein respond?
o: Show that "game" does not fit such a definition
Agree, since every concept can be defined
Say that concepts do not exist
Ignore the claim because it is only a word game
questions.why: The game example is his challenge.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by "meaning is use".
questions.model: The meaning of a word is largely found in how it is used in the practices and contexts of speakers, not in a mental object or fixed definition.
questions.why: He said "for a large class of cases", not all.

questions.q: Why is the question about continuity between early and late Wittgenstein debated?
o: Some stress breaks and others stress themes that persist
He wrote only one book, so there can be no change between phases
He wrote no books at all
He never changed his views in his life

panel.q: Why might the family-resemblance idea matter in law or science?
o: Categories may have fuzzy edges
Words never change in meaning over time
Laws should be written as poems
Science has no use for categories

panel.q: Why would a purely private language have trouble supplying correctness standards?
panel.model: If only the speaker could check, there would be no independent way to tell correct use from merely seeming correct, so the idea of a rule lapses. This is one reading.

panel.q: How could "meaning is use" be criticised?
o: It may not cover every kind of meaning
It proves that language does not exist
It forbids the use of dictionaries
It is a claim about numbers
panel.why: Critics ask about reference and truth.

teach.model: Early Wittgenstein held that propositions picture facts. Later he said meaning is use in language-games and concepts like "game" have family resemblance. He criticised the idea of a purely private language. For example, no single feature defines all games.

stages.title: G. W. F. Hegel and dialectical philosophy
stages.hook: A master depends on a servant for work, and the servant gains skill through that work. Who is more dependent in the end? Think about it.
explain: G. W. F. Hegel (1770 to 1831), a German philosopher, built a large system in which reason unfolds in history. In the Phenomenology of Spirit (1807) he traced how consciousness develops by meeting contradictions and moving beyond them. His method is often called dialectical: a position meets its opposite or tension and is transformed into something richer. The familiar triad "thesis, antithesis, synthesis" is popularly attached to Hegel but is not his own formula; scholars prefer terms such as determinate negation and sublation (Aufhebung), which both cancels and preserves.

A famous passage, the "master and bondsman" (lordship and bondage), says self-consciousness needs recognition from another. The master gets recognition from someone he does not regard as an equal, which is hollow, while the bondsman transforms the world through labour and gains self-awareness. Hegel linked freedom with mutual recognition in institutions such as family, civil society and the state in the Philosophy of Right (1820).

He also argued that history shows the development of freedom, a view criticised as teleological and Eurocentric: his lectures contain dismissive and racist claims about Africa and other regions that are rejected today. Left Hegelians such as Marx took the dialectic in a materialist direction; Kierkegaard rejected the system; analytic philosophers often found his writing obscure. Whether Hegel's concept of "Spirit" is metaphysical or social is debated.

example.q: Explain the master-bondsman dialectic in a sentence.
steps: The master wants recognition.
He gets it from a person he treats as a thing.
The bondsman shapes the world by work and grows self-aware.
Dependence reverses.
example.a: True recognition requires mutual recognition between equals.

analogies.home: A king depends on the cook, who gains skills the king lacks.
analogies.farm: A landlord depends on workers who understand the land better than he does.
analogies.tech: A manager who relies on a system others built may not understand it.

stages.mnemonic: Hegel: opposites collide, and what survives is richer and bigger.
terms: A process of development through tension, opposition and resolution.
Aufhebung: a movement that cancels, preserves and raises up.
Being acknowledged as a free self by another free self.
Hegel's term for the shared, historical structures of mind and culture.

misc.wrong: Hegel's dialectic is just thesis, antithesis, synthesis.
misc.right: That triad is a later simplification and is not Hegel's own phrase; he spoke of determinate negation and sublation.

stages.limits: Hegel's writing is notoriously difficult and open to rival readings (metaphysical or social), and his remarks on Africa and other peoples are rightly criticised.

trip.prompt: Find the master-slave (lordship and bondage) section.

questions.q: What is the key point of the master-bondsman passage?
o: Self-consciousness requires mutual recognition
Masters are always happier than servants
Labour is meaningless for the one who does it
Servants should obey their masters without question
questions.why: Hollow recognition from a dependent cannot satisfy.

questions.q: The triad "thesis, antithesis, synthesis" is...
o: A later simplification not Hegel's own formula
Hegel's own main slogan, found in all his books
A phrase from the Philosophy of Right
A phrase taught by Aristotle in his logic

questions.q: What does Aufhebung (sublation) involve?
o: Cancelling, preserving and raising up
Only deleting an earlier idea
Only repeating an earlier idea
Only guessing at a later idea
questions.why: It has multiple senses at once.

questions.q: Which book contains the master-bondsman section?
o: Phenomenology of Spirit
Critique of Pure Reason
Leviathan
Republic

questions.q: How did Marx relate to Hegel?
o: He took the dialectic in a materialist direction
He ignored Hegel's work completely
He copied Hegel's dialectic exactly
He was Hegel's own teacher at university and took over his chair

questions.q: Hegel linked freedom with...
o: Mutual recognition in social institutions
Being alone and detached from society and other persons altogether
Nature rather than society
Wealth and property

questions.q: Match thinker with reaction to Hegel.
pairs: Rejected the system for the individual

questions.q: A critic says Hegel's philosophy of history is Eurocentric. What evidence supports this?
o: His dismissive claims about Africa and other regions
His love of experimental science and respect for all peoples' learning
His rejection of the dialectic
His praise for all cultures equally

questions.q: How does the bondsman gain self-awareness in Hegel's story?
questions.model: By working on the world and shaping things, the bondsman sees his own agency and skill in the product, gaining a sense of independence, while the master only consumes.

questions.q: Why is "Spirit" interpreted in different ways?
o: Hegel's text is dense; some read it metaphysically, others socially
He wrote nothing about Spirit
It is a ghost or supernatural being that moves through history
It is a number in his logic

panel.q: Why might mutual recognition be better than domination for a free self?
o: Recognition from equals is meaningful, while recognition from the dominated is hollow
Domination guarantees real satisfaction to the master over time
Recognition from anyone is equally valuable
Equality between persons is impossible

panel.q: Give an example from modern life of a relationship that lacks mutual recognition and say what is missing.
panel.model: An employee treated as a tool without a voice lacks recognition as a free person, so the relationship is dominated and unsatisfying even for the superior.

panel.q: Which claim best captures a charitable view of Hegel's dialectic?
o: Concepts develop by working through internal tensions
Ideas are fixed and unchanging, so history only repeats the same ones
Disagreement is useless for thought
History is a random series of events

teach.model: Hegel described development through tensions that are overcome and preserved. In the master-bondsman story, true self-consciousness needs mutual recognition. The thesis-antithesis-synthesis triad is a later simplification. For example, a boss relying on a worker.

stages.title: Karl Marx and social philosophy
stages.hook: If your work belongs to someone else and its products are sold by them, how might that change how you feel about your work? Explain.
explain: Karl Marx (1818 to 1883), a German philosopher and economist, wrote with Friedrich Engels The Communist Manifesto (1848), and later Capital (1867). His approach, historical materialism, holds that how a society organises production (its economic base) strongly shapes its law, politics and ideas (the superstructure). History, in his analysis, is shaped by class struggle, such as between those who own the means of production and those who sell their labour.

In his early Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts (written 1844) he described alienation under capitalism: workers are alienated from the products of their labour, from the activity of working, from their human potential ("species-being"), and from each other. In Capital, he argued that capitalists extract surplus value, the value workers produce beyond their wages. He also discussed ideology, ideas that justify the interests of the dominant class. In the Theses on Feuerbach he wrote that philosophers have only interpreted the world; the point is to change it.

Marx's ideas have been influential across economics, sociology and politics, and are interpreted in many ways. Critics point to difficulties with the labour theory of value, to forecasts that did not occur, and to the record of states that claimed Marxist inspiration; defenders reply that those states departed from his ideas or that his analysis of capitalism remains useful. Philosophers also compare Marx with liberal accounts of freedom and justice. Here the aim is to understand the arguments, not to endorse them.

example.q: A factory worker assembles one part all day and never sees the finished product. Which Marxian idea applies?
steps: Work is controlled by others.
The product is not theirs.
The worker is alienated from the product and the activity.

analogies.city: A call-centre worker follows scripts and targets set by others; Marx would ask whether the work expresses their own capacities.
analogies.farm: A tenant farmer works land owned by another and gives up part of the harvest.
analogies.tech: A platform worker uses an app that sets prices and tasks without their say.

stages.mnemonic: Marx: Who owns the means? Who works? Who gains the surplus?
terms: The view that economic production shapes social and political life and history.
Conflict between groups defined by their relation to production.
Estrangement of workers from their products, work, nature and each other.
Ideas that present the interests of a dominant group as natural or universal.
In Marx, value produced by labour beyond the wage paid.

misc.wrong: Marx wrote a blueprint for a one-party state.
misc.right: Marx wrote little about the detailed form of a future society; how his ideas relate to later regimes is debated.

stages.limits: Marx is interpreted very differently: as economist, philosopher, sociologist or revolutionary. Critiques include the labour theory of value, predictions and later political history.

trip.prompt: Find alienation and historical materialism in the article.

questions.q: Historical materialism says...
o: Economic production strongly shapes society and ideas
Ideas alone shape the economy, while production has no real influence
History is a random series of events
Nature controls society and nothing else
questions.why: Base shapes superstructure, with debate on strength.

questions.q: Alienation in Marx refers to...
o: Workers' estrangement from product, work and others
Workers moving abroad to find better jobs and a new life there
People leaving a political party
Students studying mathematics alone
questions.why: Four forms are listed in the 1844 Manuscripts.

questions.q: Surplus value is...
o: Value produced beyond wages
A tax paid by workers to the state
A bonus paid to workers at year's end
A holiday granted to workers
questions.why: It is the source of profit in Marx's theory.

questions.q: What is ideology in Marx's sense?
o: Ideas that serve the interests of a ruling group
Any belief that a person happens to hold, true or false, in private
A tool used by workers in a factory
A branch of natural science

questions.q: Who co-wrote The Communist Manifesto?
o: Friedrich Engels
Georg Hegel, the philosopher
John Stuart Mill, the economist
Jean-Jacques Rousseau, the theorist

questions.q: The 11th Thesis on Feuerbach says philosophers have...
o: Only interpreted the world; the point is to change it
Ruled the world through ideas, and now the world must be left alone
Ignored the world around them
Abolished the world as it stands
questions.why: This is Marx's remark about practice.

questions.q: Which is a common criticism of Marx's theory?
o: The labour theory of value is disputed
He wrote no books on economics
He never lived in any city
He opposed all thought about society

questions.q: Match concept and illustration.
pairs: Worker never sees the finished product
Owners and workers in conflict over wages
Ideas that make a system seem natural

questions.q: Explain how historical materialism treats the relation between economy and ideas, and one criticism.
questions.model: It claims the way production is organised strongly shapes laws, politics and ideas. Critics say it is too deterministic, because ideas and culture can also shape the economy.
questions.why: Marxists debate how strong the determination is.

questions.q: A student says "Marx predicted all communist states". What is wrong?
o: Marx wrote little about detailed post-capitalist institutions, and later regimes differed
He wrote the constitutions of those states before he died in 1883
He founded each of those states himself
He was alive when they were created
questions.why: Their relation to his ideas is contested.

panel.q: Which statement presents Marx neutrally for study?
o: A major thinker whose analysis of capitalism is both influential and contested
A saint whose ideas must be accepted without any question or criticism
A villain whose ideas should be dismissed
A fictional figure in political writing

panel.q: Compare Marx's critique of capitalism with a liberal defence in one sentence each.
panel.model: Marx argues capitalism alienates and exploits workers under class power, whereas liberal defenders argue that markets protect freedom of choice and promote prosperity.
panel.why: Each side has more detailed arguments.

panel.q: How does Marx connect philosophy and action?
o: He urges analysis to inform changing society
He rejects all action in favour of thinking
He holds that only thinking matters
He wanted all books banned

teach.model: Marx argued that the organisation of production shapes society and ideas, that class conflict drives change, and that under capitalism work can be alienating. His ideas are widely debated. For example, a worker who never sees the finished product.

stages.title: Jean-Paul Sartre and existentialism
stages.hook: A waiter plays his role so perfectly that he seems more like an actor than a person. Is he free to stop? Is he fooling himself?
explain: Jean-Paul Sartre (1905 to 1980), a French philosopher, novelist and playwright, developed existentialism in Being and Nothingness (1943) and the lecture Existentialism Is a Humanism (1946). His slogan is that existence precedes essence: for humans there is no fixed human nature given in advance; we exist first and define ourselves through our choices.

This means radical freedom and responsibility. Even in difficult situations, Sartre argued, we always can choose how to respond, so we cannot excuse ourselves by blaming nature, society or God. This produces anguish, awareness of the weight of choice. People often flee this through bad faith (mauvaise foi), self-deception such as treating oneself as a fixed thing: the waiter who is nothing but a waiter, or someone who says "I have no choice, that is just how I am." Sartre also described the look of the other, which can make me feel myself an object, and wrote in the play No Exit that "hell is other people", a line he later said was often misunderstood.

Critics argue that Sartre overstates freedom and neglects social structures that limit options; Simone de Beauvoir, for example, stressed the situation in which freedom is exercised. Others question whether his claim that humans lack any nature is consistent. Sartre was also politically engaged, supporting leftist causes, and declined the 1964 Nobel Prize. His thought is sometimes read as a call to authenticity, owning one's choices.

example.q: A student says "I cannot study, I am just a lazy person." How would Sartre describe this?
steps: It treats a choice as a fixed nature.
It excuses the person from responsibility.
That is bad faith.
example.a: Bad faith: denying one's freedom and responsibility.

analogies.sport: A player says "I'm just not a team player" as if it were fixed, rather than a choice they keep making.
analogies.home: A parent says "I'm just built this way", avoiding the choice to change.
analogies.music: A musician who chooses a style each time acts freely, unlike a recording that repeats the same.

stages.mnemonic: Existence first, essence after; choose, own it, avoid bad faith.
terms: The claim that humans first exist and then define themselves through choices.
Self-deception that denies one's freedom or treats oneself as a fixed thing.
Awareness of the weight of responsibility for one's choices.

misc.wrong: Sartre said everyone can do whatever they like with no limits.
misc.right: Sartre said we are always free to choose our response to our situation, which includes limits ("facticity"), and that choices carry responsibility.

stages.limits: Critics (including Beauvoir) argue Sartre's early picture of freedom underplays social constraints. Sartre revised some views later.

trip.prompt: Find existence precedes essence and bad faith.

questions.q: Existence precedes essence means...
o: Humans define themselves through choices
Objects exist before people do
Essences are fixed by nature
Gods decide what each person will be
questions.why: Contrast with a tool designed for a purpose.

questions.q: Bad faith is...
o: Self-deception about one's freedom
Lack of religious faith
Telling a lie to another person
A kind of anger at others

questions.q: Anguish in Sartre is...
o: Awareness of the weight of one's choices
Pain from a physical injury or the fear of being hurt in an accident
A holiday feeling of release
A mood connected to weather

questions.q: Which is an example of bad faith?
o: "I have no choice, that's how I am."
"I decided and accept the consequences."
"I want to study."
"I will try."

questions.q: "Hell is other people" appears in...
o: No Exit
Being and Nothingness only
The Republic
Walden
questions.why: It is a line from a play.

questions.q: Sartre refused which award in 1964?
o: The Nobel Prize in Literature
The Booker Prize for fiction
A title in chess
The Fields Medal in mathematics

questions.q: Match term and meaning.
A critic says "A person born into poverty cannot just choose differently." What is the best Sartrean reply?
o: Situation limits options but not the freedom to choose a stance within them
Poverty is not real, so the problem raised by the critic disappears
Everyone is rich enough to choose freely
Choice is impossible for the poor

questions.q: Explain why Sartre thinks blaming one's "nature" can be a form of self-deception.
questions.model: Because he holds that we have no fixed essence and keep choosing who we are, appealing to a fixed nature treats a choice as a thing and avoids responsibility.
questions.why: Critics ask whether character and circumstances limit choice more than Sartre allows.

questions.q: Which question marks the limit of Sartre's radical freedom?
o: How much do social structures constrain real options?
How many colours can the human eye tell apart in good light?
What is two plus two?
Where is the city of Paris?

panel.q: How does existentialism differ from the view that human nature is fixed by biology or God?
o: It denies a given purpose that precedes choices
It agrees that human nature is fixed
It denies that people ever make choices
It is mainly a theory about cooking and food

panel.q: A student claims Sartre promotes selfishness. How could you respond?
panel.model: Sartre argued that in choosing for myself I also affirm a picture of humanity for others, so choices carry responsibility toward everyone, which is not simple selfishness.
panel.why: He made this point in his 1946 lecture.

panel.q: Why is authenticity a demanding ideal?
o: It means owning choices without excuses
It is easy, since choices are automatic
It requires being rude to others
It requires great wealth
panel.why: It asks for honesty with oneself.

teach.model: Sartre said existence precedes essence: we define ourselves through our choices. This brings freedom, responsibility and anguish. Bad faith is denying that freedom. For example, saying "I can't help it, that's just who I am."

points.ask: What does existence precedes essence mean?

stages.title: Simone de Beauvoir and ethics
stages.hook: Are the qualities society attaches to girls and boys given by nature or learned? How would you investigate?
explain: Simone de Beauvoir (1908 to 1986), a French philosopher and writer, published The Ethics of Ambiguity (1947) and The Second Sex (1949). In The Second Sex she asks why women have been treated as secondary: man is taken as the standard (the Subject) and woman as the Other. Her famous line is that one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman: many features of womanhood, she argues, come from social situation and education, not from biology alone.

Beauvoir uses an existentialist framework. Humans are free beings who project themselves into the future (transcendence), but circumstances can confine people to repetition (immanence). Women, she argued, have often been pushed toward immanence by laws, customs and expectations, so their freedom is limited by situation. In The Ethics of Ambiguity she argues that human existence is ambiguous (both free subject and physical, finite being) and that a free person who wills their own freedom must also will the freedom of others; oppressing others contradicts it.

Beauvoir's work shaped feminist philosophy. Critics have asked whether she undervalued women's experiences of embodiment, whether her view of freedom is individualistic, and how well it applies across cultures and classes; later feminist thinkers expanded these points. Her relationship and exchange with Sartre are discussed, but scholars stress her independent philosophical contributions.

example.q: A society tells girls they are "naturally" bad at maths, and fewer study it. How would Beauvoir analyse this?
steps: It describes a social situation, not just nature.

example.a: Social expectations shape and limit, not biology alone.

analogies.home: A family gives different chores by gender without asking what each child wants.

The social and material conditions in which a person is free to act.
The human condition of being both free subject and bodily object.
Being confined to repetition and maintenance rather than projecting into new aims.

misc.right: She discussed biology at length but argued it does not by itself determine social meanings.

stages.limits: Scholars debate her views on the body, motherhood and universality, and later feminists such as Judith Butler and others have built on and criticised her ideas.

stages.title: Hannah Arendt and political philosophy
stages.hook: A clerk follows orders so completely that he never thinks about what the orders do. Can that be a serious failing? Why?
explain: Hannah Arendt (1906 to 1975), a German-born political thinker who fled Nazi Germany and later lived in the United States, wrote The Origins of Totalitarianism (1951), The Human Condition (1958) and Eichmann in Jerusalem (1963). She analysed totalitarian regimes as new forms of rule that used terror and ideology to destroy the space for individual spontaneity and plurality.

From observing the trial of Adolf Eichmann, an organiser of deportations in the Holocaust, she coined the phrase "the banality of evil". She did not claim evil is ordinary or that Eichmann was innocent. She meant that he seemed to act from thoughtlessness and careerism, failing to think about what he was doing, rather than from monstrous motives. Historians and philosophers later argued that Eichmann was more committed to Nazi ideology than she allowed, and debate continues about her portrayal.

In The Human Condition she distinguishes labour (meeting life's needs), work (making lasting things) and action (acting and speaking together in public among equals). Action is tied to natality, the human capacity to begin something new. For Arendt, politics requires a public space where people appear to one another, and she warned that losing citizenship removes "the right to have rights". She was criticised on several of her claims, yet she remains central to political theory.

example.q: Why does Arendt warn that "thoughtlessness" can enable harm?
steps: People may follow orders without judging.
They may avoid asking what their acts cause.
So thinking and judging are a safeguard.
example.a: Refusing to think about consequences can enable harm.

analogies.city: Citizens meeting in a public square to discuss a law are acting politically in her sense.
analogies.home: A family that can speak freely about a decision includes everyone as a voice.
analogies.tech: A platform that connects strangers into public conversation could support action; one that silences voices could undermine it.

stages.mnemonic: Arendt: think, judge, act together, and begin anew.

Arendt's phrase for grave wrongdoing arising from thoughtlessness rather than monstrous motives.

misc.right: She held him fully responsible; "banality" concerned his motives, not guilt.

stages.limits: Historians dispute her portrayal of Eichmann, and critics debate her distinctions (such as between the social and the political) and her comments on other topics.

stages.title: Michel Foucault and power
stages.hook: A school adds cameras, timetables, grades and rankings. Does this only restrict students, or does it also shape what kind of people they become?
explain: Michel Foucault (1926 to 1984), a French philosopher and historian of ideas, studied how knowledge, institutions and power shape human subjects. In works such as Discipline and Punish (1975) and The History of Sexuality (from 1976), he traced how practices in prisons, clinics, schools and other institutions produce categories of people and ways of understanding ourselves.

He argued that power is not only a ruler saying "no". Modern power also operates through routines, observation, measurement and norms. In Discipline and Punish he used Jeremy Bentham's panopticon (a design where inmates might be watched at any time without knowing) as a model of how being observable leads people to regulate themselves. He wrote about power/knowledge: forms of knowledge (such as psychiatry or criminology) both depend on and support relations of power. He also introduced biopower, the management of populations and life, as in public health and statistics.

Foucault used genealogy, historical analysis of how present practices came to be, to show that what seems natural may have a contingent history. He insisted that where there is power there is resistance. Critics ask whether his view leaves room for universal norms and for judging when power is unjust, and some historians dispute details of his accounts. Foucault himself resisted labels such as structuralist or postmodernist. This lesson explains ideas, not endorses them.

example.q: A workplace tracks employees' keystrokes and displays a ranking. How would Foucault describe this?
steps: Observation and measurement shape behaviour.
People adjust without being told.
It is disciplinary power operating through norms.

analogies.city: CCTV in a street can change behaviour even when nobody watches the screen.
analogies.home: A family chart of chores with stars shapes behaviour through visible comparison.
analogies.tech: A fitness app scores users and nudges them to keep up, which is a norm-setting tool.

misc.wrong: Foucault said power is always bad and should be removed.
misc.right: He said power is everywhere in social relations and can be productive; the question is how it operates and what it does, and resistance is possible.

stages.limits: Foucault's methods and claims are debated by historians, and critics ask what normative standards he can use, which he partly addressed in later work on ethics and self-care.

stages.title: John Rawls, Robert Nozick and theories of justice
stages.hook: You design the rules of a society without knowing whether you will be rich or poor, healthy or sick, in the majority or a minority. What rules would you choose?
explain: John Rawls (1921 to 2002), in A Theory of Justice (1971), argued that principles of justice are those that free and equal persons would agree to in a fair starting position, the original position, behind a veil of ignorance: they do not know their class, talents, race, sex or conception of the good. Since they do not know where they will end up, they would choose principles that are fair to all.

Rawls argued that they would choose two principles: first, equal basic liberties for all; second, social and economic inequalities are acceptable only if they come with fair equality of opportunity and if they benefit the least advantaged (the difference principle). Critics from the left say he accepts too much inequality; communitarians say he ignores shared values; some argue that people would choose to maximise average welfare instead of the worst-off.

Robert Nozick (1938 to 2002), in Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), offered a rival libertarian view: justice is about entitlements. If holdings are justly acquired and justly transferred, the resulting distribution is just, and only a minimal state limited to protecting against force, theft and fraud is justified. His Wilt Chamberlain example argues that any pattern of distribution is disrupted by free exchanges, so enforcing a pattern violates liberty. Critics question his account of initial acquisition and whether holdings now reflect just histories. These are live debates, and neither view is simply correct.

example.q: Why does the veil of ignorance help?
steps: It stops choosers favouring their own position.
So they pick rules acceptable from any position.
This is meant to model fairness.

analogies.city: A city designing a housing policy chooses fairer rules if planners do not know which home they will get.
analogies.sport: A league sets fair draft rules before knowing which team they will manage.
analogies.home: The person who cuts the cake does not know which slice they get, so cuts evenly.

stages.limits: This is a live disagreement; neither view is settled. Both are debated by egalitarians, libertarians, communitarians and others.
